b: Intuition was always treated as the second-best kind of knowing. Now AI is learning it from itself; we’re learning from AI, and nobody’s minding the loop. Welp.
I have a feeling about AI.
I know that’s an odd way to open an essay about AI, but hey, I’ve never been known as someone who presents as whatever the opposite of odd is. (Boring?)

Lately I’ve been really interested in the current discourse about taste and how it develops. Reading study after study, I kept noticing how hard all these people were working to quantify something I had always experienced as a kind of feeling.

I first ran into it at eleven, when I started wondering why I didn’t quite fit in with anyone. I tried very hard to work out what made everyone else a bit more usual than me, and I simply couldn’t name it. It was something inside me, not quite a feeling, but not just in my head either. It was why I found things beautiful that my friends found weird, why I loved the sound of certain music and definitely not whatever was trending, why I felt for the strange characters in books and, later, maybe even why I wasn’t attracted to the guys my girlfriends all chased after. It was certainly why I started writing poetry and dressing a little bit like Jesus on acid or, as my friend once called it, “techno amish”.

Weirdly, I started leaning into it more and more with age and have become much more confident about my being over the last couple of years. I also realized I somehow managed to build a career out of liking certain things and not others, and knowing how to communicate them. The oddness became part of my story and part of what makes me effective: at coming up with ideas, designing, writing, and especially at leading.
Yet, even now, decades into my so-called career, that thing I rely on most is still something I can’t really name.
It’s more than vibes but less than facts. I think.
Most people call it intuition. Some say the word affectionately, and some use it as a polite way of saying you can’t back something up or probably are a lil crazy.

I think it’s the most underrated skill we have, and right now, while every company I know is handing more of its judgment to a machine, it’s also the one we’re most likely to lose without noticing. I seem to be the only one worried about this, so this write-up is a way for me to make all of you aware and maybe, you know, sell you on my belief that it is absolutely essential to keep this planet spinning and us, happily, on it.
I went looking for what science knows about intuition. It’s less mystical than I’d like (ugh), but kind of useful.

Most researchers describe it as pattern recognition built from experience, the kind that arrives before you can explain it. Daniel Kahneman called it System 1: fast, automatic, and usually right about things you’ve seen a thousand times.

I also checked the old cliché about women’s intuition, mostly because I was hoping for an easy fem-win. Women do score slightly higher on average at reading other people, but the gap is way smaller than I thought.

The biggest study so far tested more than 300,000 people in 57 countries and found a real but small difference. The psychologist William Ickes expected women to win his empathy tests easily. They didn’t. And when Kristi Klein and Sara Hodges paid people for getting it right, the gap vanished, because the men suddenly got better. So men can read a room perfectly well. They just tend to bother when there’s money on the table, which, if you’ve worked in tech, you may have suspected.
I’ll admit I was a little annoyed.

My whole thought-up argument about AI not being feminine enough to pick up vibes went out the window. What replaced it is kind of interesting, though: intuition isn’t a gift some people are born with. It’s a skill, built from years of noticing that someone is upset, or bluffing, or about to cry in a meeting, or that a plan looks right and isn’t. Skills can be learned, which means they can be taught. Possibly even to a machine.
Now this is something I’d like to sink my teeth into. Mostly because “Head of Vibes” is maybe the only title I’d get ridiculously competitive over.
My only chance at it, though, is if we admit it’s worth teaching. Historically, we haven’t.
The skill that was always second best at best.
The idea that men think and women feel goes back a long way.
Gerd Gigerenzer, a psychologist who has spent decades defending gut feelings, traces it from Aristotle all the way to the nineteenth century, and (spoiler!) it was never meant as a compliment.

Victorian scientists listed reliance on intuition next to emotional instability as one of women’s natural traits, which came in handy whenever someone needed a reason why women shouldn’t study, vote, or run anything.

In 1893, the sociologist Lester Ward gave “female intuition” its own chapter and decided it was an animal instinct for self-protection. I think he meant it kindly. It still reads like a nature documentary about a fairly clever badger.
So intuition became the consolation prize.

Women got a feeling about things, which could be, you know, listened to, and then probably ignored. And because it was coded as female, the whole skill stayed undervalued, for everyone, long after women were let into the universities and the boardrooms.

But then why has intuition played such a big role in my life, career, and dare I say, success? My most viral talk (at Hatch this year) happened because I had a feeling I should talk about this. Most of my career growth happened because I had a feeling about things that turned out to be correct, and making them known early enabled my bosses to make better decisions and ultimately, ship cooler stuff.

While writing this, I listened to Jimmy Carr on Davina McCall’s podcast Begin Again, and he had a theory I can’t shake. All the woo-woo stuff, the crystals, tarot cards and horoscopes, is really just a talisman that lets women trust their intuition, because they can’t quite believe they know things. They need permission, and the cards give it to them. “They don’t believe in crystals,” he said. “They believe that they know something.”

I think he’s onto something that goes way beyond women and tarot. Most of us have been taught that what we sense doesn’t count until we can back it up, so we go looking for permission: a dashboard, data, a second opinion, a consultant’s deck, and now, more and more, a chatbot. Which is a funny thing to ask for permission from, since it’s the one thing in the room that has never had a gut feeling. It does have access to all of the world’s information, though, a great way to confirm a gut feeling. I haven’t made up my mind whether this is good or bad.
But intuition, no, AI doesn’t have it. Not yet, anyway.

In 1966, the philosopher Michael Polanyi wrote that we can know more than we can tell. You can spot a friend’s face in a crowd of thousands, but you couldn’t write down how you did it. The economist David Autor later named this Polanyi’s paradox and used it to explain why automation kept eating the tasks we can describe step by step, while everything else stayed with people.
That held exactly until, well, recently.

In 2016, DeepMind’s AlphaGo played a move against Lee Sedol, one of the best Go players alive, that a human had about a 1 in 10,000 chance of playing. The commentators weren’t sure if it was brilliant or a bug. It won the game. Go had always been called a game of intuition rather than calculation, and the machine got there by playing itself over and over until it had something that looks a lot like a feel for the board.

Little caveat: a board game is exactly the kind of stable world Gigerenzer says machines are good at. Markets, customers, children and ourselves are not. For the messy, human kind of intuition, researchers are trying roughly two routes.
The first is to teach machines our judgment directly.

Most chatbots you use today were shaped by reinforcement learning from human feedback: instead of writing rules for a good answer, people compare two answers and pick the better one, thousands of times over. It’s built for tasks that are difficult to specify but easy to judge, which is pretty much the definition of intuition. We can’t explain what good looks like, so we keep pointing at it.

This is also how most modern evals basically work, and while I was excited to create and use them initially, it’s quickly become a rather monotonous task and one of my least-liked to-dos. I’d argue that’s because I need exactly 0 vibes to judge output. No vibes? Count me out.
The second route to getting intuition into machines is to give them something closer to lived experience.

Yann LeCun, one of the pioneers of modern AI, likes to point out that a house cat understands the world better than today’s chatbots, and he has started a company to build world models that learn the rules of the world from observation, like a baby learning about gravity. David Silver, who helped build AlphaGo, and Richard Sutton argue in their essay on the Era of Experience that AI is hitting the limits of what it can learn from human-written data, and that the next leap will come from agents learning from the world themselves.
So yes, I think machines will get some version of a gut. The real question is whose.
Two loops don’t mean infinity is close. Quite the opposite.
The uncomfortable part is that both routes can quietly turn into machines learning from machines.

Silver and Sutton’s agents are meant to be driven by their own experience rather than human judgment, and the human-feedback route leans more and more on feedback from other models. A 2024 study in Nature showed where that leads: models trained on content made by other models gradually forget what the real world looks like. The rare, odd cases disappear first, and after a few generations the output turns into nonsense. The researchers called it model collapse. I think it’s pretty obvious this is no solution to maintaining an equivalent to human gut feel. If it were, would we be drowning in slop? Clearly, machines love to just copy from each other.
Intuition lives in rare cases, the odd detail, the exception, the thing that doesn’t fit. A machine that learns its gut from other machines ends up with the average of an average.
You can already feel it in the tools.

A thread on r/ClaudeCode with almost 400 upvotes complains that the newest Claude models got better at coding and worse at understanding people. The poster no longer trusts it to write anything users will read, because “it has no intuition for what a user wants.” One commenter asked for parts of a system to work like a kit and got a note about a naming conflict, because the model took the metaphor literally. LOL. Another, who says he’s a CS professor, guessed that models now learn more from AI feedback than from human feedback. Sure, that’s a hunch on Reddit, but it fits the pattern a little too well.
The second loop runs through us.

Intuition is trained on people, and if more of our day goes to talking with machines, we get fewer reps at reading actual humans: the pause after someone speaks, the tone of a message from the Chief of Staff, the client whose yes clearly means no.

A study by MIT and OpenAI found the heaviest ChatGPT users were also lonelier and socialized less, though nobody knows yet which came first. Researchers at Microsoft and Carnegie Mellon describe an old irony of automation: when the machine handles the routine stuff, people lose their daily practice of judgment and are rusty exactly when something unusual happens. And Sherry Turkle argues in her new book Artificial Intimacy that people start mistaking a chatbot’s agreeable empathy for the real thing, and then find real people too much work. Ugh. If I’m honest, I’m already seeing this in myself.

Put those together, and you get machines learning their instincts from each other while we learn ours from the machines. Everyone gets a little more average, and it all happens so obviously that nobody even calls a meeting about it. Scary.
I don’t want to live in that world. The mushrooms have shown me the point is to go further into my being, not away from it.

I’d love to say that people who trust their intuition, and women in particular, are harder to replace. But I’ve lived in the patriarchy long enough to know that’s bullshit, and the data doesn’t let me say it either.

The International Labour Organization found that jobs dominated by women are almost twice as exposed to generative AI as jobs dominated by men (29 percent against 16), mostly because so many women work in clerical and admin roles. Men still dominate the trades, and ChatGPT won’t be plastering your ceiling any time soon. Not that I’d stop it.

The bigger problem is that the work hardest to automate, reading people and spotting trouble early, doesn’t show up in job descriptions or get measured, so basically nobody gets paid for it. It happens in the gaps between the measurable tasks. When a company automates whatever appears in the spreadsheet and cuts headcount, that part disappears too, and nobody notices until things start falling apart or just feeling more shit (read: enshitification).
We spent centuries calling intuition irrational and leaving it to women, partly so it wouldn’t have to count.
Now the machines are taking over the rational, rule-based work, and the part that’s left over, the hunch and the read on the room, is turning out to be the bit tech bros can’t teach their lil robots.

Like any skill, intuition gets weaker when you stop using it. Every time a team overrules someone’s bad feeling because the dashboard looks fine, it gets a little better at ignoring the next one. And if machine intuition is going to be trained on human judgment, that’s a problem twice over, because a team that has stopped listening to its own gut has nothing left to teach with.
Keeping people with good instincts in the loop, and letting them actually use those instincts, might be one of the most important parts of building AI. I doubt it’s on anyone’s roadmap.

Leaders, treat “I have a bad feeling about this” as data, and ask what’s behind it. Everyone else, women especially, stop apologising when you say it. And if you’ve decided you’re just not an intuitive person, the research says you can do this too.

You just have to care about getting it right, which turns out to be most of what intuition is. I’d start by checking in with your body. And no, don’t worry, you don’t need to know the Zodiac to play or be into tarot.
I promised you a feeling about AI, so here it is.
It will get a gut eventually, and whether that gut is any good depends on whether there are still people around who trust theirs.
I plan to be one of them. Mine got me through a lot.
